newsitem.title: USA: Appeals court says IRS can tax buyers of bad bonds.
newsitem.headline: Appeals court says IRS can tax buyers of bad bonds.

text.p: In a legal blow to the tax-exempt bond market, a federal appeals court has ruled that the IRS can tax the interest on muni bonds that were, without investors' knowledge, issued improperly, according to a 12-page decision.

Bondholders will ask the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit to rehear the precedent-setting case, Harbor Bancorp vs. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, shortly, investors' attorney Mary Reichert told Reuters on Thursday.

The case dates back to 1993 when the Internal Revenue Service declared as taxable roughly $30 million in bonds originally sold by a Riverside County, Calif. housing authority to build two multifamily housing projects.
The Whitewater Garden Apartments were never built. The Ironwood Apartments were constructed, but not with bond proceeds.

Both deals were rushed to market on Dec. 31, 1985, by New York City underwriter Matthews & Wright to beat a new federal curb on "arbitrage" -- profits made by selling tax-exempt bonds and reinvesting proceeds in higher-yielding bonds.
The Securities and Exchange Commission later revoked Matthews & Wright's broker-dealer license after concluding that the Dec. 31 bond closings were a "sham" because no cash actually changed hands.

IRS moved to collect nearly $68,000 in back taxes on the interest that investors earned from the deals. But investor attorneys said bondholders should not be punished because neither they nor the housing authority knew of the wrongdoing.
The U.S. Tax Court rejected the arguments, and the ninth circuit appeals panel sitting in Pasadena this week upheld that decision.
The three-judge panel said there were ways that bond issuers could have checked on whether the Dec 31 bond closings were legitimate.
They could have wire transferred the $30 million in funds or used a cashier's or certified check, instead of the less secure checks they relied on, the court said.

The panel noted that investors had argued that the IRS' position is overly harsh. They also predicted dire results if governmental issuers had to account for unauthorized investments by bond professionals, the court said.
But the court said nothing in the legislative history for 1985 or 1986 federal laws setting arbitrage rebate standards indicates Congress intended to protect investors in such cases, the court said.

Perhaps this ruling will encourage bond issuers to keep "tight control" over bond proceeds and better protect the interests of those buying their securities, the court said, citing an earlier argument by IRS.

Reichert said, "They basically said we agree with the bondholders that the statute is ambiguous, but we must defer to the (IRS) commissioner's interpretation. Well, that's brand new law as far as I'm concerned and everyone else at Bryan Cave, because that's not the law."
She continued, "There are 100 (IRS) audits pending now. This says if the government comes in and says your bonds are taxable, this court's going to say we've got to defer to the commissioner."
